source.title: Identification & interpretation of playing styles in the National Football League (NFL)

paper.citation: Carter B., James N., Parmar N. Identification & interpretation of playing styles in the National Football League (NFL). International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport. 2026;:1-20. doi:10.1080/24748668.2026.2682075.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Can offensive and defensive playing styles be empirically identified from NFL technical performance variables, and how strongly are the resulting latent styles related? Participants: No human participants; 1,311 NFL regular-season games yielding 2,622 team-game observations. Sport and level: Professional American football. Design: Retrospective observational performance-analysis study. Exposure or intervention: Aggregated team-game technical and situational variables; no intervention.
paper.tldr: Optimal coordinates retained eight components explaining 57% of variance across 2,622 team-game observations; parallel analysis suggested 10 components but the two additional features added only about 2% variance. The eight components were interpreted as passing efficacy, deep passing, scrambling, rushing, passing efficiency under pressure, coverage, defensive disruption, and tackling. The eight-component structure is best treated as a candidate feature map for film, self-scout, and opponent-analysis workflows.
paper.methods: Design: Retrospective observational performance-analysis study. Exposure or intervention: Aggregated team-game technical and situational variables; no intervention. Comparator: Covariation among 46 candidate variables and correlations among extracted components. Measurements and outcomes: Public play-by-play indicators spanning passing, rushing, scrambling, coverage, disruption, and tackling. Analysis: Correlation-based principal component analysis, KMO and Bartlett suitability tests, parallel analysis and optimal coordinates for retention, and direct-oblimin rotation; loadings below |0.32| were excluded from interpretation.
paper.findings: Optimal coordinates retained eight components explaining 57% of variance across 2,622 team-game observations; parallel analysis suggested 10 components but the two additional features added only about 2% variance. The eight components were interpreted as passing efficacy, deep passing, scrambling, rushing, passing efficiency under pressure, coverage, defensive disruption, and tackling. Passing efficacy and deep passing accounted for 12% and 9% of total variance, respectively; scrambling and rushing each accounted for 8%. The defensive-disruption component loaded most strongly on sacks (0.61), tackles for loss (0.51), and interceptions (0.47), while the tackling component was marked by rushing broken tackles (0.60) and defensive missed tackles (0.58). Only one component correlation was described as meaningful: passing efficacy and deep passing correlated at 0.35; the remaining styles were largely uncorrelated.
paper.limitations: Public play-by-play data emphasize actions by or toward the ball carrier and omit important off-ball, blocking, spacing, and interaction information. The input set was uneven: passing components represented 48% of proportional explained variance, rushing/scrambling 29%, and defensive features 23%. Component selection and naming depend on retained variables, rotation, loading thresholds, and analyst interpretation; some factors may be areas of performance rather than stable “styles.” The study did not validate component stability out of sample, link styles to winning or future behavior, or test decision utility. NFL patterns from 2018–2022 require explicit replication before transfer to current NFL seasons or collegiate American football. Team-game aggregation can obscure opponent, score, down-distance, personnel, and game-state effects.
paper.practicalImplications: The eight-component structure is best treated as a candidate feature map for film, self-scout, and opponent-analysis workflows. Before operational use, a collegiate program should rebuild the inputs from its own definitions, stratify by game situation and personnel, test year-to-year and opponent-adjusted stability, and validate whether the scores improve a concrete decision. Component labels should support analyst conversation, not be mistaken for causal mechanisms or forecasts.
